summary: Makes the AES Key Wrap algorithm conveniently available to the Internet community. Its text is largely taken from a NIST draft. The algorithm is meant for encrypting other cryptographic keys with an AES key.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes one secret key must be sent inside a protected envelope. This document describes a standard way to lock one key using another with AES.

subtitle: How to encrypt one cryptographic key with another using AES, with a built-in integrity check.

tldr.problem: Keys and other short secrets often need to be encrypted with another key, and the result must reveal tampering and be longer than one 128-bit AES block if needed.
tldr.mechanism: The AES Key Wrap splits the key data into 64-bit blocks, adds a 64-bit integrity register starting at a constant, and runs 6n AES steps over them. Unwrapping reverses the steps and checks that the constant came back.
tldr.outcome: A wrapped key can be unwrapped only if the check value matches, otherwise an error is returned and no key data. Protecting the key-encryption key from disclosure remains the user's job.

today: RFC 3394 is an Informational RFC from September 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Terms
sections.content:
RFC 3394 makes the AES Key Wrap algorithm conveniently available to the Internet community. Most of the text is taken from a NIST draft, and the document states that its security assertions are made by the US Government, not by the authors.

The goal is to use AES as a primitive to securely encrypt plaintext keys together with associated integrity information, such that the combination could be longer than the 128-bit AES block size. The data being wrapped is called the key data, though the algorithm does not care whether it is really a key. The key doing the wrapping is the key-encryption key (KEK), which can be a 128-bit, 192-bit or 256-bit AES key.
sections.plainLanguage: You have a secret and a stronger secret to lock it with. This note explains the exact steps for locking and unlocking.

sections.title: How the Algorithm Is Set Up
sections.content:
The wrap operates on blocks of 64 bits. The key data is parsed into n blocks of 64 bits, and the only restriction is that n be at least two. For key data of 64 bits or less, the constant and the key data already form a single 128-bit codebook input, so key wrap is unnecessary. No upper bound is placed on n.

The same description serves all three KEK sizes. The key size changes the overall security, not the algorithm. The process takes s = 6n steps, and the output is n+1 64-bit blocks, one more than the input.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret is cut into small pieces, and the same shuffling trick is used whether the lock key is short or long.

sections.title: Wrap and Unwrap
sections.content:
Wrapping starts with a 64-bit register A set to the initial value and registers R[1] to R[n] holding the key data blocks. For each of the 6n steps, the algorithm encrypts A joined with the first block under the KEK, XORs the step number t into the upper 64 bits to become the new A, and keeps the lower 64 bits as the new last block. The output is A followed by the blocks.

The RFC gives two equivalent descriptions: a register-shifting form and an index-based form that can run in place. The test vectors use the index-based form.

Unwrapping runs the steps in reverse, using AES decryption. At the end it checks the recovered A. If it is an appropriate initial value, the blocks are returned as the plaintext. Otherwise an error is returned.
sections.plainLanguage: Each round scrambles the pieces and mixes in a counter. Unlocking undoes every round backwards.

sections.title: The Integrity Check and Initial Value
sections.content:
The initial value (IV) is the value of A[0]. It gives the integrity check: after unwrapping, the recovered A[0] is compared with the expected value. If it matches, the key is accepted, and if not, it is rejected.

The default IV is the hexadecimal constant A6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6. When unwrapping yields that value, the chance that the key data is corrupt is 2^-64. Any other value means the unwrap must return an error and not return any key data.

Alternative initial values are allowed for cases where the integrity scope needs to be broader or the data is not a multiple of 64 bits. The RFC says NIST will define alternatives in future key management publications, so general implementations need flexibility in how the IV is set and tested.
sections.plainLanguage: The box starts with a secret stamp. If the same stamp is there when you open it, nobody tampered with it.

sections.title: Identifiers, Test Vectors and Security
sections.content:
NIST assigned object identifiers for the algorithm with the default IV, one per KEK size: id-aes128-wrap, id-aes192-wrap and id-aes256-wrap, defined as { aes 5 }, { aes 25 } and { aes 45 }.

Section 4 gives full worked test vectors for six combinations of key data and KEK size, from 128 bits of data with a 128-bit KEK up to 256 bits of data with a 256-bit KEK. They show every step for both wrapping and unwrapping, so implementers can check their code.

The security section repeats that a failed check MUST return an error and MUST NOT return any key data. It also says implementations must protect the KEK from disclosure, because compromise of the KEK may disclose all key data protected with it.
sections.plainLanguage: There are sample runs to check your work. The one big rule is to guard the lock key, because it opens everything it locked.
